results.title: DBS Reskills 11,000 Staff as AI Reshapes Banking Jobs
results.description: DBS has already upskilled more than 11,000 employees whose roles are being significantly reshaped by artificial intelligence. Now, Singapore’s largest bank is stepping up its workforce transformation – while making a notable pledge: «save people, not jobs.» DBS is deepening its efforts to prepare employees for the impact of artificial intelligence, signing an industry-first agreement with the Institute of Banking and Finance Singapore (IBF) to jointly develop AI skills and help workers transition into redesigned roles. The Memorandum of Understanding is the first of its kind between IBF and a financial institution and covers three areas: building foundational AI capabilities, reskilling employees whose roles are changing and strengthening the pipeline of young talent entering Singapore’s financial industry. DBS has already equipped all 40,000 employees globally, including 14,800 in Singapore, with foundational AI skills. More than 11,000 employees working in roles significantly reshaped by AI have also undergone upskilling. «Save people, not jobs» The initiative comes as banks globally grapple with the implications of generative AI for their workforces. DBS is positioning the technology primarily as a means of augmenting employees rather than simply replacing them. «We see AI as a cognitive enhancer – augmenting what people can do by automating the mundane, taking away repetitive and administrative tasks,» said Lee Yan Hong , Head of Group Human Resources at DBS. By freeing employees from such tasks, AI should create more capacity for higher-order skills including critical thinking, problem solving and relationship building, she added. DBS’ approach to the transformation is encapsulated in a particularly pointed principle. «Our philosophy has always been to save people, not jobs,» Lee said. «Jobs will change and tasks will evolve, but we are determined to bring everyone along our workforce transformation.» The bank’s ambition, according to Lee, is to become an «AI-enabled bank with a heart», with humans remaining in the lead as work evolves. AI governance and prompt engineering Under the partnership, DBS and IBF will equip employees with foundational competencies including AI governance, responsible AI, prompt engineering and practical applications of the technology. The two organizations will also test workforce interventions aimed at employees whose jobs are being reshaped by AI. This will draw on IBF’s Job Redesign and Reskilling Career Conversion Programme as well as DBS’ experience with its existing workforce transformation. The partnership extends beyond the bank itself. DBS and IBF intend to jointly develop programs that can build AI capabilities across Singapore’s broader financial services industry. Carolyn Neo , CEO of IBF, described DBS as a «lighthouse financial institution» in showing how employees can be supported alongside the adoption of AI. Human advisors for an AI-driven workplace At the same time, DBS is adding a distinctly human component to its technology-driven workforce strategy. The bank has launched a Career Advisory Service with an initial pool of more than 100 career advisors drawn from within DBS. The service will initially be available to employees across the bank’s six core markets. It combines human career guidance with two of DBS’ existing AI-powered tools. iGrow, launched in 2022, uses AI and machine learning to recommend learning opportunities and potential jobs based on an employee’s skills, career aspirations and learning history. iCoach, introduced in 2025 in collaboration with executive coach Marshall Goldsmith, uses generative AI to provide personalized coaching and career guidance. Building the next generation DBS and IBF are also targeting younger workers as the skills required by the financial industry change. Their collaboration includes IBF’s Young Talent Programme for AI in Finance, in which DBS is a pioneer partner. The bank has committed to taking in more than 500 young local talents in 2026 through its Management Associate, Internship and Traineeship programs. The initiative effectively turns DBS’ own experience with AI-driven workforce transformation into a potential blueprint for Singapore’s wider financial sector – at a time when banks are increasingly having to determine not only where AI can boost productivity, but what that means for the people currently doing the work. results.title: How Weak RPO Enforcement Is Harming India's Renewable Growth? Study Explains
results.description: India’s renewable energy compliance framework continues to face weak enforcement, fragmented regulatory processes and growing legal ambiguity, according to a new discussion paper by Prayas (Energy Group) assessing the implementation of Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPO) and Renewable Consumption Obligations (RCO). The paper, “Fragmented Frameworks and Entangled Enforcement: Assessing the implementation of RPO and RCO”, published in August 2026, argues that the introduction of the RCO framework alongside the existing RPO mechanism has added another layer of institutional complexity without resolving the long-standing enforcement gap. Under the Electricity Act, 2003, State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) are required to specify RPOs for obligated entities, while penalties can be imposed for non-compliance. However, the paper finds that although most SERCs monitor and report RPO compliance, only a small number regularly impose penalties. Enforcement is described as episodic rather than systematic, with significant differences in penalty approaches between states. Compliance Gap Significant The scale of the compliance gap remains significant. The paper estimates that renewable energy, including large hydro and captive generation, accounted for around 25.7% of total electricity consumption in FY 2025-26 against an RPO target of 33%. This represents an estimated shortfall of 138 billion units and a 7.3 percentage-point gap against the target. The report also highlights the growing overlap between RPO under the Electricity Act and RCO under the Energy Conservation Act. The two frameworks have different statutory bases, target-setting authorities and compliance mechanisms, while SERCs continue to play a role in penalties. According to the paper, this has resulted in uncertainty over applicable provisions, institutional responsibilities and enforcement pathways. RCO Buy Out Price Another concern is the RCO buy-out mechanism. The paper argues that if buy-out remains relatively inexpensive compared with direct renewable procurement, it could become a de facto compliance route rather than a last-resort mechanism, weakening the incentive to contract renewable capacity. It recommends strict conditions and a sunset provision for the buy-out option. Prayas recommends simplifying the RPO-RCO framework under a single Act, imposing time-bound compliance and verification processes, ensuring consistent collection of penalties, restricting routine carry-forward and waivers, and publicly disclosing compliance and penalty data. It also calls for clearer delineation of responsibilities among SERCs, the Bureau of Energy Efficiency and state agencies. The paper concludes that the principal constraint is no longer policy design but enforcement. With renewable energy and energy storage costs declining, it argues that stronger and more consistent regulatory enforcement is essential for translating India’s renewable energy targets into actual deployment.

results.title: Drone attack kills two children, burns logistics hub in Russia's Krasnodar
results.description: Two children were killed and another nine people, including seven children, ​were injured after drone debris hit a private ‌childcare centre in Krasnodar, southern Russia, overnight, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said. In Ukraine, a Russian attack on the outskirts of the northeastern ​city of Kharkiv killed three people, the governor said ​on Telegram late on Sunday. Ukraine is seeking additional ⁠interceptor missiles from the US and Europe, its ​key allies, to repel such attacks, in its fifth year ​of war with Russia. Debris fell on apartment buildings and warehouses caught fire in Krasnodar, Kondratyev said on the Telegram messaging app. The ​attack caused a fire at a logistics hub ​of Russian online retailer Ozon, the company said on Telegram. In Russia’s Nevinnomysk, a ‌chemical ⁠production area in the Stavropol region next to Krasnodar, a drone attack on an industrial area was repelled, Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said on Telegram early on Monday. Ukraine has ​stepped up attacks ​on logistics ⁠hubs and warehouses across Russia, bringing the war which Russia started in February 2022 closer to ​ordinary Russians, some of whom make their ​living ⁠from selling goods online. In comments published on Saturday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Kyiv had opened a “Pandora’s box” with ⁠its strikes ​on Russian economic targets and ​that Moscow would hit back at Ukraine’s “most sensitive economic sectors”.

results.title: Ethical home accessories brand Nkuku teams with Back.tech to rethink returns across business
results.description: Back.tech is partnering with Nkuku to improve how it manages consumer returns, reverse logistics and recommerce. In a LinkedIn post, Giorgio Vitale, Co-founder and CRO at Back.Tech, said: "A big part of what makes this special is Operations & Impact Director Chris Wilson’s vision for reverse logistics at Nkuku - moving beyond current state returns processing to a smarter, connected reverse lifecycle for every product." "This means rethinking returns across the full operation: DTC e-commerce - streamlined parcel returns; Big and bulky items - smarter grading, routing and resale decisions; B2B supplier returns - improved visibility and control upstream to optimise downstream requirements; Recommerce - maximising value through quicker resale and redistribution. This is exactly where we add new value." Back.tech's AI powered grading and dynamic routing engine helps businesses accurately assess condition, automate decisioning, and optimise where every item should go next. For Nkuku, this will improve reverse logistics performance by: Reducing operating costs through automation and fewer manual decisions; Improving delivery and handling efficiency across return flows; Unlocking net savings by routing items to the highest value recovery path faster and more accurately; Increasing recovery rates across both parcel and bulky inventory streams." 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Returns will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards . The awards are now open for entries and celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November. Check out our 2025 winners here . Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson . In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.” “But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.” He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.” Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel , the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.
